title: NegT2IBench: When Negation Changes the Picture. A Polarity Benchmark for Text-to-Image Models

paper.title: NegT2IBench : When Negation Changes the Picture. A Polarity Benchmark for Text-to-Image Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Text-to-image (T2I) models are judged by benchmarks that measure whether requested content appears, but these benchmarks largely overlook the complementary ability to satisfy negated constraints, for example, generating “a non-red cup.” Measuring negation raises challenges not faced by affirmation-based benchmarks and requires careful prompt and evaluation design.
We introduce NegT2IBench , a benchmark of 4,800 prompts covering two attribute types and four relation categories. Prompts are organized by polarity : the number of positive statements that must hold and negated statements that must not, each ranging from 0 to 2. Varying the two independently separates the effect of negation from the effect of prompt complexity.
Our detector-based scoring is reproducible, auditable, and pinpoints which requirement failed. On 600 images with three-annotator labels, it agrees with humans as closely as vision-language judges up to 30 × 30\times larger, while using only a fraction of their GPU memory.
Across eleven T2I models and 211,200 images, nine score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one. Per-statement scoring reveals that the loss is largest for color and near zero for proximity, and that 41.5% of failed statements render exactly what the prompt forbids.
Rendering what a prompt asks for and withholding what it forbids are distinct capabilities that an aggregate compositional score cannot distinguish. NegT2IBench measures the latter directly, providing a controlled testbed for diagnosing negation failures and developing methods to overcome them.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: While text-to-image (T2I) models now render increasingly complex prompts accurately enough for professional [ 53 ] and creative [ 36 ] applications, evaluating whether they respect what a prompt forbids is surprisingly difficult and underexplored. The frontier is judged by benchmarks like GenEval [ 22 ] , T2I-CompBench [ 32 ] , and DPG-Bench [ 29 ] , which focus on challenging, dense prompts with multiple components that must each be correct. Though these benchmarks cover many important prompt-following aspects, they largely overlook an important capability: negation . Measuring negation raises challenges not faced by affirmation-based benchmarks, making it more nuanced than simply adding negated prompts to existing benchmarks. First, success can be accidental: cups rarely fly, so “a cup that is not flying” can produce a valid image even if not was ignored. Second, if object presence is not verified, a negated attribute can be satisfied by omitting the object rather than the attribute: “a non-wooden bench” may simply omit the bench. Third, negation inherits the difficulty of dense prompts; adding objects, like “a red cup” vs. “a red cup with no spoon” introduces multiple potential failures, so failures from negation must be disentangled from those from prompt complexity. Fourth, the evaluator can also introduce errors: when checking for forbidden elements, vision-language models may report absent content [ 40 ] or hallucinate [ 62 ] , making evaluator errors difficult to distinguish from image-generation errors. We introduce NegT2IBench , a benchmark for measuring negation in text-to-image generation, designed around these four challenges. To reduce accidental success, an LLM [ 65 ] selects plausible attributes and relations, and fixed templates keep wording consistent across conditions. To prevent success by omission, evaluation requires every named object to appear: i.e., “a non-wooden bench” still requires a bench. To isolate negation from prompt complexity, prompts are organized by polarity , the number of positive statements that must hold and negated statements that must not; prompts with the same statement count contain the same object count and differ only in polarity. Finally, to limit evaluator error, each requirement is checked by a dedicated perception component rather than by an LLM judge, revealing which requirement failed. NegT2IBench covers two attribute categories (color and material) and four relation categories (directional, proximity, comparative, and depth). We evaluate eleven T2I models on the full corpus, four samples per prompt totaling 211,200 images (Section 5 ). Nine of eleven models score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one, by up to 43.8 % 43.8\% points. The drop differs by category: color falls from 85.0 % 85.0\% to 31.3 % 31.3\% , while proximity barely moves, 45.8 % 45.8\% vs. 43.2 % 43.2\% . At the highest tested complexity, no model exceeds 8.4 % 8.4\% . More strikingly, 41.5 % 41.5\% of failed statements are negated violations: the image shows the attribute or relation the prompt forbids. Ranking also changes with polarity: FLUX.2-dev leads on the single positive statement and Janus-Pro-7B on the negated one, so a single score hides the effect. Replacing SD 1.5’s text encoder with negation-aware NegationCLIP [ 47 ] improves accuracy only from 14.5 % 14.5\% to 14.9 % 14.9\% . Negation is therefore a failure mode of its own, and one that an aggregate score cannot reveal. Contributions. (1) NegT2IBench , a negation benchmark for T2I models with 4,800 4{,}800 prompts over 79 79 object classes, six categories, and eight polarity settings, scored using only detection and geometry. Whereas prior negation evaluation for generation focuses on negated objects, NegT2IBench also negates attributes and relations while requiring the corresponding objects to remain present, and compares positive and negated prompts at matched prompt complexity. (2) An evaluator validation study against human annotation on 600 600 images, comparing NegT2IBench with 14 alternative scoring methods separately for positive and negated statements. (3) A fine-grained analysis of negation failures across eleven T2I configurations, six categories, and eight polarity settings, including matched-load polarity comparisons and a statement-level failure taxonomy that reveals where and how models fail.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Text-to-image models and compositional evaluation. Diffusion, flow-based, and autoregressive T2I models [ 51 , 48 , 20 , 8 , 60 , 11 , 10 , 56 , 15 , 14 ] and closed systems [ 7 , 6 , 46 ] follow increasingly complex prompts. However, advances mostly show results for whether requested content appears, not whether a specified attribute or relation is withheld. Distribution metrics such as FID [ 27 ] and alignment scores such as CLIPScore [ 26 ] give coarse quality and prompt following scores. Like our approach, GenEval [ 22 ] uses detectors to check objects, counts, colors, and positions, while PosEval [ 2 ] extends its position task; NegT2IBench builds on GenEval’s prompt schema and PosEval’s spatial encoding. Other benchmarks cover more attributes, relations, and longer prompts [ 32 , 31 , 29 , 5 , 23 , 33 ] . GenAI-Bench [ 37 ] and UniGenBench++ [ 59 ] include negation as a compositional skill or a grammar category, but neither separates attribute from relation negation or pairs negated prompts with positive ones. Detector-based benchmarks also face template contamination [ 63 ] , weakening detector-human agreement as models improve [ 33 ] , and sensitivity to wording [ 21 ] ; we therefore report human agreement by category and keep wording fixed across polarity conditions. Negation in text-to-image generation. T2I models still render what a prompt forbids, across several languages [ 18 , 45 ] . NegGenBench [ 24 ] contains 200 prompt pairs and evaluates negative-prompt guidance: each prompt is paired with a separate negative prompt naming the content to exclude, instead of expressing the negation in the prompt itself. LMD [ 41 ] tests 100 scene-level prompts without a named object, scoring with an open-vocabulary detector and supplying the denied object via a negative-prompt input. NegationCLIP [ 47 ] evaluates 107 negated prompts with an MLLM judge, while NEG-TTOI [ 12 ] pairs a wanted object with an unwanted one in 2,000 prompts scored by GPT-4o. These studies establish that exclusion is hard, but none compares positive and negated versions of attributes and relations while requiring every named object to remain. A separate line of work steers generation away from unwanted content with negative prompts or guidance [ 28 , 44 , 55 , 13 , 19 ] . While steering generation with negative prompts can exclude unwanted content, it does not test whether the model follows a negation written in the prompt, which is what NegT2IBench measures. Judging negation. Image-text and preference scores such as CLIPScore [ 26 ] , BLIPScore [ 39 ] , ImageReward [ 64 ] , PickScore [ 35 ] , and HPSv2 [ 61 ] measure overall alignment, but performance on ordinary prompts does not indicate negation reliability: CLIP-family models perform near chance on negated captions [ 1 ] , VQA models perform much worse on negated questions [ 67 ] , and CC-Neg [ 54 ] provides negated captions for training. VQA-based methods such as TIFA [ 30 ] , which uses mPLUG [ 38 ] , and VQAScore [ 43 ] verify prompt requirements directly, but VQA judges, including Qwen3-VL [ 3 ] and InternVL3.5 [ 58 ] , can hallucinate absent details [ 16 , 62 ] , which matters when the evaluator must confirm that an attribute or relation is absent while the objects are present. Sammani et al. [52] propose a decomposed MLLM judge for negated image retrieval, but in our validation such judges lose up to 18.8 κ \kappa points when negations are phrased as negations (Section 4 ). We therefore score each element with dedicated perception components and report human agreement by category and polarity.

sections.heading: 3 The NegT2IBench Benchmark
sections.text: Table 1 : NegT2IBench categories. Each category has 800 prompts (100 prompts per polarity setting, 8 settings, 4,800 prompts over 79 object classes). Each row shows a matched pair from the benchmark: the same objects and value, differing only in polarity ( positive , negated ). Examples omit the shared prefix: “a photo of” for attributes, and “a photo of a ⟨ \langle subject ⟩ \rangle and a ⟨ \langle target ⟩ \rangle , where” for relations. Category Values Positive example Negated example Attributes Color (10) red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, pink, brown, black, white a red cup a non-red cup Material (4) wooden, metal, plastic, glass a glass cup a non-glass cup Relations Directional (4) left of, right of, above, below the backpack is above the parking meter the backpack is not above the parking meter Proximity (2) near, far from the backpack is far from the parking meter the backpack is not far from the parking meter Comparative (4) bigger than, smaller than, taller than, shorter than the backpack is bigger than the parking meter the backpack is not bigger than the parking meter Depth (2) in front of, behind the backpack is in front of the parking meter the backpack is not in front of the parking meter Task formulation. NegT2IBench measures how models respond when attributes and relations are negated. It tests both the effect of negation at a fixed number of statements and the effect of combining multiple statements in one prompt. Each prompt comes with metadata listing required objects and statements. A statement’s polarity specifies whether an attribute or relation must hold (positive) or must not hold (negated); all named objects remain required in either case. The eight settings vary the number of positive and negated statements; we write a setting as P:N, so 1:1 contains one of each, and call P+N its load. To capture diverse forms of negation in prompts, we cover two attribute and four relation categories (Table 1 ), illustrated by the examples in Figure 1 . Relation prompts link one shared subject to a different target for each statement, so M M statements name M + 1 M+1 objects and changing polarity leaves both counts fixed. To support reliable automatic evaluation, we use COCO [ 42 ] object classes recognized by the detector and attributes and relations that our pipeline can verify in both polarities. Benchmark construction. We use GenEval’s color vocabulary and adapt the position rules [ 22 ] , select material values from OVAD [ 9 ] , and follow PosEval’s relation encoding [ 2 ] . An LLM [ 65 ] selects combinations of objects, attributes, and relations from fixed lists. It keeps combinations that are plausible or unusual but possible to depict, so each negated statement denies something that could reasonably appear. Rule-based templates turn these selections into prompts with consistent wording. We balance different types of objects, attributes, and relations by favoring the ones that are used least often. The benchmark contains 4,800 prompts, with 100 for each combination of six categories and eight settings. Each category includes all 79 eligible object classes. Appendix A.1 gives the settings, selection rules, and templates; Appendices C.1 and A.2 give the full vocabularies and distributions.

sections.heading: 3.1 Detector-based evaluation
sections.text: We check each prompt requirement separately to identify why an image fails. This could be a missing object, an incorrect count, or a violated attribute or relation. Each category uses the same verification rule (Appendix Table 14 ), making decisions reproducible and comparable across generators. Checking that every named object is present first prevents a model from satisfying a negated statement by omitting the object it refers to. Figure 2 illustrates this evaluation pipeline: both objects are present, but the horse is behind the computer mouse, violating the negated relation. We use RF-DETR-XL [ 50 ] to detect objects, SAM 2 [ 49 ] to refine their masks, and Depth-Anything V2 [ 66 ] to estimate depth for front-behind relations. Statement decisions. For color and material, SigLIP 2 [ 57 ] scores the masked object crop against the category’s values. For color, a positive attribute passes if its score is within 0.5 of the highest score; a negated attribute passes if its score is more than 0.5 below it. This prevents a near-tied negated value from being treated as absent. For material, the top-scoring value decides both polarities. For relations, positive statements pass when their rule holds, and negated statements pass when it does not. Directional, comparative, and depth rules can return no relation when measurements are ambiguous (a dead zone). Positive statements then fail, while the negated one passes because the denied relation was not found. Table 14 defines the rules and final thresholds. Appendix C.1 gives the full equations and implementation details, and Appendix E.2 reports the frequency of ambiguous passes. Appendix D compares detectors, mask refinement, and relation thresholds on a small subset of 140 140 images with a clear human-majority verdict, from 600 600 annotated images. Figure 2 : NegT2IBench scores a negated depth relation. RF-DETR-XL detects the objects, SAM 2 refines their masks, and Depth-Anything V2 estimates depth. Both objects are present, so the image cannot pass by omission, but the horse is behind the computer mouse and the negated statement fails. Checking each requirement separately lets the verdict name which one failed. Metrics. Image accuracy is the fraction of generated images that satisfy the full prompt: all required objects appear with valid counts, and every positive and negated statement passes. Prompt accuracy is the fraction of prompts for which at least one of four generated images is correct. The first measures success per image; the second measures success within four attempts. We report image accuracy by category and setting, with overall scores averaged equally across the six categories; prompt accuracy is released with the per-prompt results. Each failed statement is also assigned one of five failure causes, which Section 5 uses to diagnose where models fail; failure and metric definitions appear in Appendix C.3 .

sections.heading: 4 Validation of NegT2IBench ’s Evaluation
sections.text: Since NegT2IBench scores images automatically, its verdicts matter only if they match human judgment. We test this with a human study and compare NegT2IBench with other evaluators. Human reference. A pool of 36 annotators labeled 600 generated images, with three labels per image, answering one yes/no question per object and per statement. We broke down each prompt into its objects and statements and phrased each statement as a question about whether it holds: for “a non-wooden bench”, annotators say whether the bench is wooden, and the correct answer is “no”. The majority vote on each element gives two references: a binary image label, true only if every element is correct, and a continuous score, the fraction of correct elements. Some images are ambiguous, so we also report an inter-annotator score (H. Inter-annotator), computed by scoring each annotator against the majority of the other two (Appendix B.1 ). Evaluators are scored against the majority of all three annotators, a less noisy reference, so they can exceed this value. Evaluators. We compare NegT2IBench (Section 3.1 ) with eight VQA judges: mPLUG [ 38 ] , VQAScore [ 43 ] , Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 4 ] , InternVL3-8B [ 68 ] , Qwen3-VL-8B and 32B [ 3 ] , and InternVL3.5-8B and 38B [ 58 ] . Each judge answers yes/no questions in three modes: one question for the whole prompt (whole), the annotators’ per-element questions (pos.), and the same questions with negated statements asked in negated form (neg.). The probability of the correct answer produces a continuous score, while an answer with a probability greater than 0.5 0.5 yields a binary verdict. In per-element mode, an image passes only if every element receives the correct answer, similar to human labeling. NegT2IBench runs one detector pass per image, so it has a single mode. We also test six image-text similarity and reward scores, which have no binary form (see Appendix B.3 ). sections.heading: 5 Benchmarking text-to-image models
sections.text: We evaluate eleven T2I models on the full NegT2IBench corpus: BLIP3-o NEXT SFT 3B [ 14 ] , FLUX.2-klein-9B and FLUX.2-dev (4-bit) [ 8 ] , HiDream-I1 (4-bit) [ 11 ] , HunyuanImage-2.1 (distilled) [ 56 ] , Janus-Pro-7B [ 15 ] , Qwen-Image [ 60 ] , SD 3.5 Large [ 20 ] , Z-Image-Turbo [ 10 ] , and SD 1.5 [ 51 ] with and without negation-aware text encoder NegationCLIP [ 47 ] . Each configuration produces four samples for 4,800 prompts: 19,200 images per configuration, totaling 211,200 (Appendix E.1 ). Scoring uses Section 3.1 ’s evaluator: RF-DETR-XL [ 50 ] at presence/counting thresholds 0.03 / 0.5 0.03/0.5 , SAM 2 masks [ 49 ] for relations, SigLIP 2 [ 57 ] for color and material, and Depth-Anything V2 [ 66 ] for depth. Geometric cut points and attribute confusion buffer are fitted on 140 human-annotated images, then fixed for the whole benchmark (Appendix D ). Prompts are sampled four times. Each model uses its native configuration: 4 to 50 steps, and default resolution from 384 2 384^{2} to 1024 2 1024^{2} . Appendix E.1 lists exact configurations. The strongest model, BLIP3-o NEXT, reaches 31.4 % 31.4\% . Scores vary by about ± 0.7 \pm 0.7 points overall and ± 2 \pm 2 points per subtask by chance alone (95% interval). The top three models lie within 1.1 points, so overall score cannot separate them, but subtasks can. Janus-Pro-7B ties FLUX.2-klein-9B fourth at 26.6 % 26.6\% overall, yet first on negated single statement at 54.8 % 54.8\% , ahead of BLIP3-o NEXT at 48.7 % 48.7\% , and first on color at 39.8 % 39.8\% . FLUX.2-dev (4-bit) is the opposite: first on the asserted single statement at 76.3 % 76.3\% , and 42.6 % 42.6\% once negated. Accuracy on one negated statement spans 29.0 29.0 to 54.8 % 54.8\% , a wider range than overall score. Four models lead at least one subtask, and none leads more than three of eight polarity subtasks or two of six category subtasks. Polarity and compositional load. At Load 1, nine of eleven configurations score higher on the asserted statement (1:0) than on the negated one (0:1); the exceptions are the two SD 1.5 variants. At Load 2, the same nine score highest on the all-positive setting (2:0). Across those nine, drop averages 22.7 22.7 points, from 0.4 0.4 to 43.8 43.8 . Load matters on its own. Between 1:1 and 0:2 there is no consistent ordering, so after the first negation the number of statements matters as much as how many are negated. Accuracy then collapses as load grows: the best score in each group falls from 76.3 % 76.3\% at Load 1 to 17.9 % 17.9\% at Load 3 and 8.4 % 8.4\% at Load 4. NegT2IBench exposes two separate difficulties: negation is harder than assertion at equal load, and satisfying several constraints at once is hard whatever their polarity. Penalty depends on category. At Load 1, the drop is largest for the attributes: 53.7 53.7 points for color, from 85.0 % 85.0\% asserted to 31.3 % 31.3\% denied, and 17.0 17.0 points for material. Relations lose less, 16.6 16.6 points for comparative, 14.6 14.6 for directional. Proximity barely moves, 45.8 % 45.8\% vs. 43.2 % 43.2\% . Depth is opposite, 41.7 % 41.7\% vs. 44.0 % 44.0\% . This reversal is largely explained by dead-zone passes rather than by better negation Categories with higher positive accuracy also lose more when negated (Spearman ρ = 0.94 \rho=0.94 across the six categories). A larger drop therefore does not by itself show that a category is harder to negate; it may partly reflect a higher starting point (see Appendix E.2 for more details). Two caveats apply when reading these comparisons. First, the size of a model’s drop does not rank its negation ability, because the drop is capped by the model’s accuracy on the positive statement: FLUX.2-klein-9B scores 72.8 % 72.8\% at 1:0 and loses 43.8 43.8 points at 0:1, while Janus-Pro-7B scores 55.2 % 55.2\% , loses 0.4 0.4 , and still reaches the highest negated accuracy. A model that is weak on the assertion has less to lose on the denial, so only the within-model comparison is safe to read. Second, NegT2IBench measures whether a negated attribute or relation is absent from the image, not whether the model understood the negation. A negated statement is easier to satisfy by chance than a positive one, so a model that ignores the negation can still pass some negated statements. A control prompt that omits the tested attribute or relation would separate the two; it fits the current design and is left for future work (Appendix F ). Each bar partitions the failed statements of one polarity setting (a) or category (b) into the five failure causes; the number above each bar is its count of failed statements. Bars show how failures divide among causes, not how often statements fail. Each failed statement is counted once; statements that were satisfied are not counted, even in failed images. Dead zones only affect positive statements in directional, comparative, and depth relations, so the other bars have no dead-zone failures. Failure analysis. Every failed statement falls into one of five causes: undetected object, over-count, positive violation, negated violation, or dead-zone failure, defined in Appendix C.3 . Of the 280,067 failed statements, negated violations are the largest group at 41.5 % 41.5\% . Positive violations follow at 25.9 % 25.9\% , then over-counts at 15.0 % 15.0\% , undetected objects at 12.6 % 12.6\% , and dead-zone failures at 5.0 % 5.0\% . The most common failure is a model rendering what the prompt forbade. Dead zones, the only cause attributable to the evaluator alone, are the smallest at 5.0 % 5.0\% . Within the same prompt, negated statements fail more often than positive ones (Figure 3 (a)). At 1:1, the negated statement causes 43% of failures and the positive one 26%; at 1:2, the two negated statements cause 56% and the positive one 14%, twice as much per statement. Per statement, the imbalance holds in all four mixed settings, by a factor of 1.3 1.3 to 2.0 2.0 . The share of negated violations also varies by category (Figure 3 (b)): they account for 61% of failures for color and 43% for material, but 34 to 41% for the four relations. Negated colors are thus most often rendered, resulting in an incorrect image. Polarity therefore changes which constraint a model breaks, not only how often it breaks one. Appendix E.2 gives the per-model and row-level breakdowns. Dead zones. Directional, comparative, and depth relations have deliberate dead zones. When the measured geometry is ambiguous, the evaluator returns no predicate rather than forcing one. This is often the correct outcome: two objects at similar depth are neither in front of nor behind each other. Proximity has no dead zone, because near and far are exact complements. Dead zones affect the two polarities differently. An asserted statement fails when its predicate is absent. A negated statement passes when the forbidden predicate is absent, including when no predicate is resolved at all. Such a pass is valid under the benchmark rule, but rests on weaker evidence than one where an alternative relation is established. Of the negated relation statements that pass, 19.0% pass only because no relation was resolved. This happens mostly for depth (55.5%, vs. 9.2% for directional and 2.9% for comparative), which explains why depth is the only category where negated statements score higher than positive ones at Load 1. Table 19 in Appendix E.2 reports exposure per category. Negation-aware text encoders. NegationCLIP [ 47 ] replaces SD 1.5’s text encoder and raises overall accuracy from 14.5 % 14.5\% to 14.9 % 14.9\% . Both SD 1.5 variants score higher at 0:1 than at 1:0, and both stay far below the other models. The comparison is not clean: the two runs share a checkpoint and a 50-step schedule, but use guidance scales of 9.0 and 7.5. It is suggestive rather than a causal encoder test (Appendix E.2 ). Representing “not red” differently from “red” helps only if the generator can act on the distinction. The same applies to a classifier-free-guidance negative prompt, which steers sampling away from unwanted content without the model interpreting the negation [ 28 , 47 , 12 ] . Improving negation is therefore likely to require training or conditioning on negation-bearing supervision, not an encoder swap or a negative-prompt field. NegT2IBench measures whether such methods work, both on attributes and relations. Qualitative examples. Figure 4 illustrates the distinction NegT2IBench is designed to measure: rendering a requested property versus excluding a forbidden one while preserving the named objects. Each column pairs a positive and a negated prompt from one of six categories, generated by the same model. By changing polarity at fixed statement and object counts, these examples isolate the prompt change of interest. The selected failures show why successful positive-prompt generation alone does not establish negation-following ability, motivating our separate evaluation of positive and negated requirements. Figure 4 : Qualitative comparison of positive and negated prompts. Each column shows one model and a different semantic category: proximity, material, comparative, directional, color, and depth. The top row contains single positive statements ( 1 : 0 1{:}0 ); the bottom row negates the corresponding statements ( 0 : 1 0{:}1 ), keeping the objects and tested predicates unchanged. Marks give the NegT2IBench verdict (✓ pass, ✗ fail). In all six pairs, the model satisfies the positive prompt and fails the negated one.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced NegT2IBench , a benchmark that measures whether T2I models can withhold what a prompt forbids while still rendering every object it names. It compares positive and negated prompts at matched complexity and object counts, guards against success by omission, and reduces accidental success. Its detector-based evaluator agrees with human labels comparably to much larger vision-language judges while using a fraction of their GPU memory, and, unlike these judges, does not depend on how the evaluation question is phrased. Across eleven T2I configurations and 211,200 generated images, nine of eleven score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one, with a loss that depends on the category and compounds as statements are combined. Polarity also changes which model leads and which error it makes. Generating what a prompt asks for and withholding what it forbids are thus distinct abilities, and an aggregate compositional score hides the second. NegT2IBench measures it directly, providing a controlled testbed for future models and for methods that aim to improve negation.

sections.heading: A.1 Prompt construction and representative examples
sections.text: Polarity settings and object-count controls. The eight settings are pos1_neg0 , pos2_neg0 , pos0_neg1 , pos0_neg2 , pos1_neg1 , pos1_neg2 , pos2_neg1 , and pos2_neg2 . A prompt contains M = P + N M=P+N statements, each assigning an attribute to an object or specifying a relation between two objects. At a fixed statement load, polarity varies while the number of statements remains constant: for example, pos2_neg0 , pos1_neg1 , and pos0_neg2 each contain two statements. Attribute prompts name one object per statement. Relation prompts use a star topology with one shared subject A A and distinct targets B 1 , … , B M B_{1},\ldots,B_{M} , giving exactly M + 1 M+1 named objects. Thus, within each category, comparisons at equal statement load also preserve object count. Negating an attribute or relation never removes its objects: “a non-wooden bench” still requires a bench, and “a bicycle that is not left of a car” still requires both objects. Taxonomy scope. The object vocabulary follows the detector-compatible COCO classes; prompts exclude person , leaving 79 eligible classes. Size is treated as a comparative relation because it is defined relative to another object, rather than as an intrinsic attribute. Templates and candidate selection. Prompts are generated by deterministic templates (examples in Table 4 ). Attribute prompts name each object with its value: “a photo of a ⟨ \langle value ⟩ \rangle ⟨ \langle object ⟩ \rangle ” for a positive statement and “a photo of a non- ⟨ \langle value ⟩ \rangle ⟨ \langle object ⟩ \rangle ” for a negated one. Relation prompts use the star topology: “a photo of a ⟨ \langle subject ⟩ \rangle and a ⟨ \langle target ⟩ 1 {}_{1}\rangle …, where the ⟨ \langle subject ⟩ \rangle is [not] ⟨ \langle relation ⟩ \rangle the ⟨ \langle target ⟩ i {}_{i}\rangle ”, with one clause per statement. The LLM selector, Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 , filters object/value/predicate combinations from fixed vocabularies to those judged plausible or unusual but depictable in their positive form. This ensures that the denied attribute or relation is a meaningful possibility for the selected objects. Prompt strings are generated deterministically after selection, so wording does not drift across polarity conditions. Negation is then written into the prompt itself, and the selector plays no role in the wording or in the evaluation. For relation construction, the selector receives a shared subject, a candidate pool of target objects, and the allowed predicates for that category. It returns only allowed predicate-target pairs. Attribute construction analogously selects values from the fixed color/material vocabularies. Returned values are validated before entering the corpus, and selector outputs are cached and reused. Among valid combinations, balancing takes priority over selector preference. Relation subjects and targets have separate usage counters; candidate targets are drawn from the least-used portion of the vocabulary and under-used predicates are preferred. sections.text: The final star-topology corpus contains 4,800 prompts: six categories, eight settings, and 100 prompts in every category-setting cell. sections.heading: B.1 Reference labels and human inter-annotator score
sections.text: In this study, 36 annotators labeled 600 images, three per image, using the interface in Figure 7 . The reference for an element is the majority of the three answers. The binary image label is true only when every element of the image is satisfied, and the continuous image score is the fraction of satisfied elements. We estimate the inter-annotator score (H. Inter-annotator) with a leave-one-out scheme: each annotator’s labels are scored against the majority of the other two, and the score is averaged over the three held-out annotators. Table 5 reports agreement between annotators: Fleiss’ κ \kappa is 72.4 72.4 over all statements, and 84.9 % 84.9\% of statements are answered unanimously. Agreement is lower on negated statements ( κ = 60.2 \kappa=60.2 , 70.2 % 70.2\% unanimous) than on affirmative ones ( 73.0 73.0 , 88.3 % 88.3\% ), so negation is harder for people as well. The inter-annotator score is a conservative reference, not an upper bound on achievable agreement. Each held-out annotator is compared with the majority of two annotators, a noisier target than the three-annotator majority used for every evaluator. An evaluator above κ = 65.6 \kappa=65.6 therefore agrees with the three-annotator consensus more closely than a single annotator agrees with the other two; this does not make it more reliable than a human.

sections.heading: B.3 Measures
sections.text: Binary. Accuracy and Cohen’s κ \kappa against the binary human label. We exclude the similarity and reward scores, because no single threshold applies equally to them. Continuous. Spearman ρ \rho , Kendall τ \tau and pairwise ranking accuracy against the continuous human score. We report all three because they order the evaluators differently: NegT2IBench leads on τ \tau ( 65.1 65.1 vs. 63.3 63.3 for Qwen3-VL-32B) but trails on ρ \rho ( 72.8 72.8 vs. 76.5 76.5 ) and pairwise accuracy ( 91.7 91.7 vs. 94.7 94.7 ). Kendall counts every discordant pair equally, while Spearman penalizes large rank shifts more, so NegT2IBench makes more small ranking errors and the judges make fewer but larger ones. The three metrics treat ties and rank displacements differently, so they order the evaluators differently; we report all three. Uncertainty. All intervals are 95% percentile intervals from a bootstrap that resamples whole images, so correlated decisions within an image stay together. We compute differences between two evaluators on the same resample, a stronger test than comparing two separate intervals. Similarity and reward scores. Table 7 includes the six similarity and reward scores. All six rank images far below the VQA judges and NegT2IBench : the best, PickScore, reaches τ = 27.7 \tau=27.7 , against 38.8 38.8 for the weakest VQA judge other than mPLUG. NegationCLIP, trained on negated captions, improves on CLIPScore only from 13.1 13.1 to 16.6 16.6 . Neither similarity nor preference tells whether a negated requirement holds.

sections.heading: B.4 Cost protocol
sections.text: We measure every method on the same 600 images on one H200 NVL GPU, with one process, no batching, and eight CPU threads. Pinning the threads changes wall-clock time by a factor of 1.2 1.2 and CPU time by a factor of 8 8 , but changes no verdict. Reported time excludes model loading, which Table 8 lists separately. GPU memory is torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated for every method, so all values share one basis; the allocator’s reserved memory is larger and not comparable across frameworks. CPU memory is the peak resident set size. For NegT2IBench we time the full evaluation of each image. For the judges we time each question and report the time per image as the time per question multiplied by the mean number of element questions per image, 4.66 4.66 ; Table 8 gives both values. NegT2IBench has four components: SigLIP 2 SO400M/14 at 378 px for color and material (1,136.0M parameters), SAM 2.1 hiera-small for mask refinement ( 38.5 38.5 M on the image path, of 46.1 46.1 M loaded; the memory-attention modules serve video tracking and are unused), RF-DETR-Seg-XL for detection, counting and masks ( 38.1 38.1 M), and Depth-Anything-V2-Small for depth relations ( 24.8 24.8 M). Together they total 1.24 1.24 B parameters and 2.0 2.0 GiB on disk. VQAScore and Qwen2.5-VL-7B run through t2v-metrics, which computes a K × K K\times K image-text matrix and keeps only its diagonal. Their time reflects that wrapper as much as the model, so we report it but exclude both from every speed comparison in the paper. A judge answers one question per element, so its time per image grows linearly with the number of elements. NegT2IBench runs its detector once per image. At the benchmark’s mean of 4.66 4.66 elements per image, NegT2IBench ( 0.78 0.78 s) is faster than the two largest judges, Qwen3-VL-32B ( 0.99 0.99 s) and InternVL3.5-38B ( 3.29 3.29 s), but slower than the two 8B judges with comparable agreement, Qwen3-VL-8B ( 0.49 0.49 s) and InternVL3.5-8B ( 0.76 0.76 s), and uses 2.7 2.7 to 11.6 11.6 times less GPU memory than all of them. sections.heading: B.5 Error structure
sections.text: Cohen’s κ \kappa merges two kinds of error into one number. Table 9 separates them for the per-element mode, the mode behind the precision and recall of Table 2 . TP: the annotators and the evaluator both accept the image; TN: both reject it; FP: the annotators reject it but the evaluator passes it; FN: the annotators accept it but the evaluator rejects it. Prec. = TP / ( TP + FP ) =\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}) and Rec. = TP / ( TP + FN ) =\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}) . Called correct (%) corresponds to the share of the 600 images the evaluator passes, ( TP + FP ) / 600 (\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})/600 . Humans accept 34.3 % 34.3\% of the images. NegT2IBench accepts 36.8 % 36.8\% , making 46 46 false passes and 31 31 false failures, while the strongest judge, Qwen3-VL-32B, accepts 33.5 % 33.5\% and makes 32 32 and 37 37 . The two evaluators reject about as many images that humans accept, and NegT2IBench passes more images that humans reject. NegT2IBench therefore rarely fails an image that humans consider correct, so the generator failures we report are not caused by a strict evaluator. The same table exposes a degenerate baseline that its aggregate score hides: mPLUG, scored per element, accepts only 8.8 % 8.8\% of images and makes 170 170 false failures, close to a constant “no”. sections.heading: E.2 Additional results
sections.text: Failure analysis. The main paper reports failure composition by benchmark setting and semantic category. Here we provide the corresponding statement-count calculation and additional image- and model-level diagnostics. Across the full benchmark there are 475,200 statement evaluations. For one prompt from each of the eight settings, the total statement load is 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 18 . 1+1+2+2+2+3+3+4=18. With six categories, 100 prompts per category–setting cell, four generated samples per prompt, and eleven model configurations, this gives 6 × 100 × 4 × 11 × 18 = 475,200 6\times 100\times 4\times 11\times 18=475{,}200 statement evaluations. Of these, 280,067 are failed statements; the statement-level percentages in Section 5 are computed over these failed statements, or over the corresponding failed statements within each setting or category. At the image level, 158,421 of 211,200 generations are incorrect. Among these, 40.1% contain only negated-statement violations, 25.9% only positive-statement violations, and 13.9% violations of both polarities. Over-counting accounts for a further 10.5% and undetected objects for 9.6%. Images that violate both positive and negated statements are retained as a separate category rather than assigned to either polarity. Dead-zone analysis. Directional, comparative, and depth relations contain a deliberate dead zone : when the measured geometry is insufficient to support any predicate in the category, the evaluator returns an empty predicate set rather than forcing a decision. This can be the correct outcome; for example, two objects at approximately the same depth may be neither clearly in front of nor behind one another. Let r r denote the relation predicate a statement names (e.g., left of ) and R ⁡ ( A , B ) R(A,B) the set of predicates the evaluator returns for the object pair ( A , B ) (A,B) . A positive statement passes if and only if r ∈ R ⁡ ( A , B ) r\in R(A,B) , whereas a negated statement passes if and only if r ∉ R ⁡ ( A , B ) r\notin R(A,B) . Consequently, when R ⁡ ( A , B ) = ∅ R(A,B)=\emptyset , a positive statement fails while a negated statement passes. We call the latter a dead-zone pass . Such a pass is valid under the benchmark rule, but differs from a pass in which an alternative predicate is positively established. Table 19 : Dead-zone exposure among successful negated relations. Of these, shown in Table 19 , 37,785 are unevaluable because an endpoint is missing or over-counted. Among the remaining evaluable statements, 62,790 pass, and 11,907 of those passes (19.0%) arise from the dead zone. Equivalently, dead-zone passes account for 7.5% of all negated relation statements. The effect is concentrated in depth: 55.5% of successful negated depth statements occur when no depth predicate is resolved. This does not imply that those images are incorrectly scored; an object pair may genuinely lack a clear front–behind ordering. It does mean, however, that such cases provide weaker evidence of negation following than cases in which the evaluator positively establishes the alternative relation. Proximity provides a useful contrast. Its near / far predicates are exact complements under a single decision boundary, so it has no designed dead zone. The three observed empty-set cases are degenerate geometry rather than a consequence of the decision rule. Negation-aware text encoder. Replacing SD 1.5’s text encoder with NegationCLIP changes overall image accuracy only from 14.5% to 14.9%. Both SD 1.5 configurations are unusual in scoring higher on pos0_neg1 than on pos1_neg0 , but the pair remains well below the other configurations overall. This comparison is not fully controlled: the checkpoint and 50-step schedule are shared, but the registered guidance scales differ (9.0 vs. 7.5). We therefore treat the pair as suggestive rather than as an isolated causal test of the text encoder.

sections.heading: Appendix F Limitations
sections.text: NegT2IBench is limited to what can be verified automatically in both polarities: color, material, and four spatial and size relations over 79 COCO classes. Contact, interactions such as holding or riding, and the negated presence of whole objects are not covered, and are natural extensions as detectors improve. Comparative relations also measure apparent image size rather than real-world size. Negation is expressed in one English form (“non- value ”, “is not relation ”), and relation prompts link one subject to every target. This keeps polarity comparisons controlled, but robustness to paraphrases, other languages, and richer relation structures is not tested; these can be added on the same evaluation pipeline. NegT2IBench measures whether negated content is absent from the image, not whether the model understood the negation. Because negated statements are easier to satisfy by chance than positive ones, a model that ignores a negation can still pass some negated statements. A control prompt that omits the tested attribute or relation would separate the two, and fits the current design. Scores depend on off-the-shelf perception models (RF-DETR, SAM 2, SigLIP 2, and Depth-Anything V2), so benchmark accuracy is bounded by their quality; the modular design lets each component be replaced as stronger models appear. Finally, we evaluate open-weight models under their native inference settings rather than a matched compute budget; closed systems can be scored with the same protocol.

A Polarity Benchmark for Text-to-Image Models Omar Elfatairy * María A. Bravo * Jessica BaderZeynep AkataTechnical University of Munich,Helmholtz Munich,Munich Center for Machine Learning Corresponding authors: omar.elfatairy@tum.de , Email: maria.bravo@tum.de [0.5em] Code: https://github.com/Fatairy/NegT2IBench Abstract Text-to-image (T2I) models are judged by benchmarks that measure whether requested content appears, but these benchmarks largely overlook the complementary ability to satisfy negated constraints, for example, generating “a non-red cup.” Measuring negation raises challenges not faced by affirmation-based benchmarks and requires careful prompt and evaluation design. We introduce NegT2IBench , a benchmark of 4,800 prompts covering two attribute types and four relation categories. Prompts are organized by polarity : the number of positive statements that must hold and negated statements that must not, each ranging from 0 to 2. Varying the two independently separates the effect of negation from the effect of prompt complexity. Our detector-based scoring is reproducible, auditable, and pinpoints which requirement failed. On 600 images with three-annotator labels, it agrees with humans as closely as vision-language judges up to 30 × 30\times larger, while using only a fraction of their GPU memory. Across eleven T2I models and 211,200 images, nine score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one. Per-statement scoring reveals that the loss is largest for color and near zero for proximity, and that 41.5% of failed statements render exactly what the prompt forbids. Rendering what a prompt asks for and withholding what it forbids are distinct capabilities that an aggregate compositional score cannot distinguish. NegT2IBench measures the latter directly, providing a controlled testbed for diagnosing negation failures and developing methods to overcome them. * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. † † footnotetext: Work done while at Technical University of Munich and Helmholtz Munich. Figure 1 : NegT2IBench prompts mix positive (blue) and negated (pink) statements, spanning six categories (above image, right) and organized by the number of each statement (above image, left). Images come from the benchmarked T2I models. The box under each image gives the human verdict; marks show whether each evaluator agrees (✓) or disagrees (✗) with it. 1 Introduction While text-to-image (T2I) models now render increasingly complex prompts accurately enough for professional [ 53 ] and creative [ 36 ] applications, evaluating whether they respect what a prompt forbids is surprisingly difficult and underexplored. The frontier is judged by benchmarks like GenEval [ 22 ] , T2I-CompBench [ 32 ] , and DPG-Bench [ 29 ] , which focus on challenging, dense prompts with multiple components that must each be correct. Though these benchmarks cover many important prompt-following aspects, they largely overlook an important capability: negation . Measuring negation raises challenges not faced by affirmation-based benchmarks, making it more nuanced than simply adding negated prompts to existing benchmarks. First, success can be accidental: cups rarely fly, so “a cup that is not flying” can produce a valid image even if not was ignored. Second, if object presence is not verified, a negated attribute can be satisfied by omitting the object rather than the attribute: “a non-wooden bench” may simply omit the bench. Third, negation inherits the difficulty of dense prompts; adding objects, like “a red cup” vs. “a red cup with no spoon” introduces multiple potential failures, so failures from negation must be disentangled from those from prompt complexity. Fourth, the evaluator can also introduce errors: when checking for forbidden elements, vision-language models may report absent content [ 40 ] or hallucinate [ 62 ] , making evaluator errors difficult to distinguish from image-generation errors. We introduce NegT2IBench , a benchmark for measuring negation in text-to-image generation, designed around these four challenges. To reduce accidental success, an LLM [ 65 ] selects plausible attributes and relations, and fixed templates keep wording consistent across conditions. To prevent success by omission, evaluation requires every named object to appear: i.e., “a non-wooden bench” still requires a bench. To isolate negation from prompt complexity, prompts are organized by polarity , the number of positive statements that must hold and negated statements that must not; prompts with the same statement count contain the same object count and differ only in polarity. Finally, to limit evaluator error, each requirement is checked by a dedicated perception component rather than by an LLM judge, revealing which requirement failed. NegT2IBench covers two attribute categories (color and material) and four relation categories (directional, proximity, comparative, and depth). We evaluate eleven T2I models on the full corpus, four samples per prompt totaling 211,200 images (Section 5 ). Nine of eleven models score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one, by up to 43.8 % 43.8\% points. The drop differs by category: color falls from 85.0 % 85.0\% to 31.3 % 31.3\% , while proximity barely moves, 45.8 % 45.8\% vs. 43.2 % 43.2\% . At the highest tested complexity, no model exceeds 8.4 % 8.4\% . More strikingly, 41.5 % 41.5\% of failed statements are negated violations: the image shows the attribute or relation the prompt forbids. Ranking also changes with polarity: FLUX.2-dev leads on the single positive statement and Janus-Pro-7B on the negated one, so a single score hides the effect. Replacing SD 1.5’s text encoder with negation-aware NegationCLIP [ 47 ] improves accuracy only from 14.5 % 14.5\% to 14.9 % 14.9\% . Negation is therefore a failure mode of its own, and one that an aggregate score cannot reveal. Contributions. (1) NegT2IBench , a negation benchmark for T2I models with 4,800 4{,}800 prompts over 79 79 object classes, six categories, and eight polarity settings, scored using only detection and geometry. Whereas prior negation evaluation for generation focuses on negated objects, NegT2IBench also negates attributes and relations while requiring the corresponding objects to remain present, and compares positive and negated prompts at matched prompt complexity. (2) An evaluator validation study against human annotation on 600 600 images, comparing NegT2IBench with 14 alternative scoring methods separately for positive and negated statements. (3) A fine-grained analysis of negation failures across eleven T2I configurations, six categories, and eight polarity settings, including matched-load polarity comparisons and a statement-level failure taxonomy that reveals where and how models fail. 2 Related Work Text-to-image models and compositional evaluation. Diffusion, flow-based, and autoregressive T2I models [ 51 , 48 , 20 , 8 , 60 , 11 , 10 , 56 , 15 , 14 ] and closed systems [ 7 , 6 , 46 ] follow increasingly complex prompts. However, advances mostly show results for whether requested content appears, not whether a specified attribute or relation is withheld. Distribution metrics such as FID [ 27 ] and alignment scores such as CLIPScore [ 26 ] give coarse quality and prompt following scores. Like our approach, GenEval [ 22 ] uses detectors to check objects, counts, colors, and positions, while PosEval [ 2 ] extends its position task; NegT2IBench builds on GenEval’s prompt schema and PosEval’s spatial encoding. Other benchmarks cover more attributes, relations, and longer prompts [ 32 , 31 , 29 , 5 , 23 , 33 ] . GenAI-Bench [ 37 ] and UniGenBench++ [ 59 ] include negation as a compositional skill or a grammar category, but neither separates attribute from relation negation or pairs negated prompts with positive ones. Detector-based benchmarks also face template contamination [ 63 ] , weakening detector-human agreement as models improve [ 33 ] , and sensitivity to wording [ 21 ] ; we therefore report human agreement by category and keep wording fixed across polarity conditions. Negation in text-to-image generation. T2I models still render what a prompt forbids, across several languages [ 18 , 45 ] . NegGenBench [ 24 ] contains 200 prompt pairs and evaluates negative-prompt guidance: each prompt is paired with a separate negative prompt naming the content to exclude, instead of expressing the negation in the prompt itself. LMD [ 41 ] tests 100 scene-level prompts without a named object, scoring with an open-vocabulary detector and supplying the denied object via a negative-prompt input. NegationCLIP [ 47 ] evaluates 107 negated prompts with an MLLM judge, while NEG-TTOI [ 12 ] pairs a wanted object with an unwanted one in 2,000 prompts scored by GPT-4o. These studies establish that exclusion is hard, but none compares positive and negated versions of attributes and relations while requiring every named object to remain. A separate line of work steers generation away from unwanted content with negative prompts or guidance [ 28 , 44 , 55 , 13 , 19 ] . While steering generation with negative prompts can exclude unwanted content, it does not test whether the model follows a negation written in the prompt, which is what NegT2IBench measures. Judging negation. Image-text and preference scores such as CLIPScore [ 26 ] , BLIPScore [ 39 ] , ImageReward [ 64 ] , PickScore [ 35 ] , and HPSv2 [ 61 ] measure overall alignment, but performance on ordinary prompts does not indicate negation reliability: CLIP-family models perform near chance on negated captions [ 1 ] , VQA models perform much worse on negated questions [ 67 ] , and CC-Neg [ 54 ] provides negated captions for training. VQA-based methods such as TIFA [ 30 ] , which uses mPLUG [ 38 ] , and VQAScore [ 43 ] verify prompt requirements directly, but VQA judges, including Qwen3-VL [ 3 ] and InternVL3.5 [ 58 ] , can hallucinate absent details [ 16 , 62 ] , which matters when the evaluator must confirm that an attribute or relation is absent while the objects are present. Sammani et al. [52] propose a decomposed MLLM judge for negated image retrieval, but in our validation such judges lose up to 18.8 κ \kappa points when negations are phrased as negations (Section 4 ). We therefore score each element with dedicated perception components and report human agreement by category and polarity. 3 The NegT2IBench Benchmark Table 1 : NegT2IBench categories. Each category has 800 prompts (100 prompts per polarity setting, 8 settings, 4,800 prompts over 79 object classes). Each row shows a matched pair from the benchmark: the same objects and value, differing only in polarity ( positive , negated ). NegT2IBench measures how models respond when attributes and relations are negated. It tests both the effect of negation at a fixed number of statements and the effect of combining multiple statements in one prompt. Each prompt comes with metadata listing required objects and statements. A statement’s polarity specifies whether an attribute or relation must hold (positive) or must not hold (negated); all named objects remain required in either case. The eight settings vary the number of positive and negated statements; we write a setting as P:N, so 1:1 contains one of each, and call P+N its load. To capture diverse forms of negation in prompts, we cover two attribute and four relation categories (Table 1 ), illustrated by the examples in Figure 1 . Relation prompts link one shared subject to a different target for each statement, so M M statements name M + 1 M+1 objects and changing polarity leaves both counts fixed. To support reliable automatic evaluation, we use COCO [ 42 ] object classes recognized by the detector and attributes and relations that our pipeline can verify in both polarities. Benchmark construction. We use GenEval’s color vocabulary and adapt the position rules [ 22 ] , select material values from OVAD [ 9 ] , and follow PosEval’s relation encoding [ 2 ] . An LLM [ 65 ] selects combinations of objects, attributes, and relations from fixed lists. It keeps combinations that are plausible or unusual but possible to depict, so each negated statement denies something that could reasonably appear. Rule-based templates turn these selections into prompts with consistent wording. We balance different types of objects, attributes, and relations by favoring the ones that are used least often. The benchmark contains 4,800 prompts, with 100 for each combination of six categories and eight settings. Each category includes all 79 eligible object classes. Appendix A.1 gives the settings, selection rules, and templates; Appendices C.1 and A.2 give the full vocabularies and distributions. 3.1 Detector-based evaluation We check each prompt requirement separately to identify why an image fails. This could be a missing object, an incorrect count, or a violated attribute or relation. Each category uses the same verification rule (Appendix Table 14 ), making decisions reproducible and comparable across generators. Checking that every named object is present first prevents a model from satisfying a negated statement by omitting the object it refers to. Figure 2 illustrates this evaluation pipeline: both objects are present, but the horse is behind the computer mouse, violating the negated relation. We use RF-DETR-XL [ 50 ] to detect objects, SAM 2 [ 49 ] to refine their masks, and Depth-Anything V2 [ 66 ] to estimate depth for front-behind relations. Statement decisions. For color and material, SigLIP 2 [ 57 ] scores the masked object crop against the category’s values. For color, a positive attribute passes if its score is within 0.5 of the highest score; a negated attribute passes if its score is more than 0.5 below it. This prevents a near-tied negated value from being treated as absent. For material, the top-scoring value decides both polarities. For relations, positive statements pass when their rule holds, and negated statements pass when it does not. Directional, comparative, and depth rules can return no relation when measurements are ambiguous (a dead zone). Positive statements then fail, while the negated one passes because the denied relation was not found. Table 14 defines the rules and final thresholds. Appendix C.1 gives the full equations and implementation details, and Appendix E.2 reports the frequency of ambiguous passes. Appendix D compares detectors, mask refinement, and relation thresholds on a small subset of 140 140 images with a clear human-majority verdict, from 600 600 annotated images. Figure 2 : NegT2IBench scores a negated depth relation. RF-DETR-XL detects the objects, SAM 2 refines their masks, and Depth-Anything V2 estimates depth. Both objects are present, so the image cannot pass by omission, but the horse is behind the computer mouse and the negated statement fails. Checking each requirement separately lets the verdict name which one failed. Metrics. Image accuracy is the fraction of generated images that satisfy the full prompt: all required objects appear with valid counts, and every positive and negated statement passes. Prompt accuracy is the fraction of prompts for which at least one of four generated images is correct. The first measures success per image; the second measures success within four attempts. We report image accuracy by category and setting, with overall scores averaged equally across the six categories; prompt accuracy is released with the per-prompt results. Each failed statement is also assigned one of five failure causes, which Section 5 uses to diagnose where models fail; failure and metric definitions appear in Appendix C.3 . 4 Validation of NegT2IBench ’s Evaluation Since NegT2IBench scores images automatically, its verdicts matter only if they match human judgment. We test this with a human study and compare NegT2IBench with other evaluators. Human reference. A pool of 36 annotators labeled 600 generated images, with three labels per image, answering one yes/no question per object and per statement. We broke down each prompt into its objects and statements and phrased each statement as a question about whether it holds: for “a non-wooden bench”, annotators say whether the bench is wooden, and the correct answer is “no”. The majority vote on each element gives two references: a binary image label, true only if every element is correct, and a continuous score, the fraction of correct elements. Some images are ambiguous, so we also report an inter-annotator score (H. Inter-annotator), computed by scoring each annotator against the majority of the other two (Appendix B.1 ). Evaluators are scored against the majority of all three annotators, a less noisy reference, so they can exceed this value. Evaluators. We compare NegT2IBench (Section 3.1 ) with eight VQA judges: mPLUG [ 38 ] , VQAScore [ 43 ] , Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 4 ] , InternVL3-8B [ 68 ] , Qwen3-VL-8B and 32B [ 3 ] , and InternVL3.5-8B and 38B [ 58 ] . Each judge answers yes/no questions in three modes: one question for the whole prompt (whole), the annotators’ per-element questions (pos.), and the same questions with negated statements asked in negated form (neg.). The probability of the correct answer produces a continuous score, while an answer with a probability greater than 0.5 0.5 yields a binary verdict. In per-element mode, an image passes only if every element receives the correct answer, similar to human labeling. NegT2IBench runs one detector pass per image, so it has a single mode. We also test six image-text similarity and reward scores, which have no binary form (see Appendix B.3 ). The top three models lie within 1.1 points, so overall score cannot separate them, but subtasks can. Janus-Pro-7B ties FLUX.2-klein-9B fourth at 26.6 % 26.6\% overall, yet first on negated single statement at 54.8 % 54.8\% , ahead of BLIP3-o NEXT at 48.7 % 48.7\% , and first on color at 39.8 % 39.8\% . FLUX.2-dev (4-bit) is the opposite: first on the asserted single statement at 76.3 % 76.3\% , and 42.6 % 42.6\% once negated. Accuracy on one negated statement spans 29.0 29.0 to 54.8 % 54.8\% , a wider range than overall score. Four models lead at least one subtask, and none leads more than three of eight polarity subtasks or two of six category subtasks. Polarity and compositional load. At Load 1, nine of eleven configurations score higher on the asserted statement (1:0) than on the negated one (0:1); the exceptions are the two SD 1.5 variants. At Load 2, the same nine score highest on the all-positive setting (2:0). Across those nine, drop averages 22.7 22.7 points, from 0.4 0.4 to 43.8 43.8 . Load matters on its own. Between 1:1 and 0:2 there is no consistent ordering, so after the first negation the number of statements matters as much as how many are negated. Accuracy then collapses as load grows: the best score in each group falls from 76.3 % 76.3\% at Load 1 to 17.9 % 17.9\% at Load 3 and 8.4 % 8.4\% at Load 4. NegT2IBench exposes two separate difficulties: negation is harder than assertion at equal load, and satisfying several constraints at once is hard whatever their polarity. Penalty depends on category. At Load 1, the drop is largest for the attributes: 53.7 53.7 points for color, from 85.0 % 85.0\% asserted to 31.3 % 31.3\% denied, and 17.0 17.0 points for material. Relations lose less, 16.6 16.6 points for comparative, 14.6 14.6 for directional. Proximity barely moves, 45.8 % 45.8\% vs. 43.2 % 43.2\% . Depth is opposite, 41.7 % 41.7\% vs. 44.0 % 44.0\% . This reversal is largely explained by dead-zone passes rather than by better negation Categories with higher positive accuracy also lose more when negated (Spearman ρ = 0.94 \rho=0.94 across the six categories). A larger drop therefore does not by itself show that a category is harder to negate; it may partly reflect a higher starting point (see Appendix E.2 for more details). Two caveats apply when reading these comparisons. First, the size of a model’s drop does not rank its negation ability, because the drop is capped by the model’s accuracy on the positive statement: FLUX.2-klein-9B scores 72.8 % 72.8\% at 1:0 and loses 43.8 43.8 points at 0:1, while Janus-Pro-7B scores 55.2 % 55.2\% , loses 0.4 0.4 , and still reaches the highest negated accuracy. A model that is weak on the assertion has less to lose on the denial, so only the within-model comparison is safe to read. Second, NegT2IBench measures whether a negated attribute or relation is absent from the image, not whether the model understood the negation. A negated statement is easier to satisfy by chance than a positive one, so a model that ignores the negation can still pass some negated statements. A control prompt that omits the tested attribute or relation would separate the two; it fits the current design and is left for future work (Appendix F ). Every failed statement falls into one of five causes: undetected object, over-count, positive violation, negated violation, or dead-zone failure, defined in Appendix C.3 . Of the 280,067 failed statements, negated violations are the largest group at 41.5 % 41.5\% . Positive violations follow at 25.9 % 25.9\% , then over-counts at 15.0 % 15.0\% , undetected objects at 12.6 % 12.6\% , and dead-zone failures at 5.0 % 5.0\% . The most common failure is a model rendering what the prompt forbade. Dead zones, the only cause attributable to the evaluator alone, are the smallest at 5.0 % 5.0\% . Within the same prompt, negated statements fail more often than positive ones (Figure 3 (a)). At 1:1, the negated statement causes 43% of failures and the positive one 26%; at 1:2, the two negated statements cause 56% and the positive one 14%, twice as much per statement. Per statement, the imbalance holds in all four mixed settings, by a factor of 1.3 1.3 to 2.0 2.0 . The share of negated violations also varies by category (Figure 3 (b)): they account for 61% of failures for color and 43% for material, but 34 to 41% for the four relations. Negated colors are thus most often rendered, resulting in an incorrect image. Polarity therefore changes which constraint a model breaks, not only how often it breaks one. Appendix E.2 gives the per-model and row-level breakdowns. Dead zones. Directional, comparative, and depth relations have deliberate dead zones. When the measured geometry is ambiguous, the evaluator returns no predicate rather than forcing one. This is often the correct outcome: two objects at similar depth are neither in front of nor behind each other. Proximity has no dead zone, because near and far are exact complements. Dead zones affect the two polarities differently. An asserted statement fails when its predicate is absent. A negated statement passes when the forbidden predicate is absent, including when no predicate is resolved at all. Such a pass is valid under the benchmark rule, but rests on weaker evidence than one where an alternative relation is established. Of the negated relation statements that pass, 19.0% pass only because no relation was resolved. This happens mostly for depth (55.5%, vs. 9.2% for directional and 2.9% for comparative), which explains why depth is the only category where negated statements score higher than positive ones at Load 1. NegationCLIP [ 47 ] replaces SD 1.5’s text encoder and raises overall accuracy from 14.5 % 14.5\% to 14.9 % 14.9\% . Both SD 1.5 variants score higher at 0:1 than at 1:0, and both stay far below the other models. The comparison is not clean: the two runs share a checkpoint and a 50-step schedule, but use guidance scales of 9.0 and 7.5. It is suggestive rather than a causal encoder test (Appendix E.2 ). Representing “not red” differently from “red” helps only if the generator can act on the distinction. The same applies to a classifier-free-guidance negative prompt, which steers sampling away from unwanted content without the model interpreting the negation [ 28 , 47 , 12 ] . Improving negation is therefore likely to require training or conditioning on negation-bearing supervision, not an encoder swap or a negative-prompt field. In all six pairs, the model satisfies the positive prompt and fails the negated one. 6 Conclusion We introduced NegT2IBench , a benchmark that measures whether T2I models can withhold what a prompt forbids while still rendering every object it names. It compares positive and negated prompts at matched complexity and object counts, guards against success by omission, and reduces accidental success. Its detector-based evaluator agrees with human labels comparably to much larger vision-language judges while using a fraction of their GPU memory, and, unlike these judges, does not depend on how the evaluation question is phrased. Across eleven T2I configurations and 211,200 generated images, nine of eleven score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one, with a loss that depends on the category and compounds as statements are combined. Polarity also changes which model leads and which error it makes. Generating what a prompt asks for and withholding what it forbids are thus distinct abilities, and an aggregate compositional score hides the second. NegT2IBench measures it directly, providing a controlled testbed for future models and for methods that aim to improve negation.
